questions.prompt: The instructor's slides line up the bacteriophage lytic cycle against the animal-virus life cycle. Which pairing is correct?

options.text: Phages are released by budding; naked animal viruses are released by exocytosis only
A phage's penetration includes uncoating; an animal virus's penetration never does
A phage can enter lysogeny instead of biosynthesis; an animal virus can enter latency instead
Animal viruses skip biosynthesis because the host already has viral proteins

questions.explanation: Slides: lysogeny ↔ latency. Animal-virus entry adds uncoating; release can be budding (enveloped), lysis (naked), or exocytosis (both).

questions.prompt: Which statement correctly contrasts a prophage, a provirus, and episomal viral DNA?

options.text: Prophage: phage DNA built into a bacterial chromosome. Provirus: animal-virus DNA built into a host chromosome (HIV). Episomal DNA: viral DNA sitting beside the chromosomes (herpes)
All three are viral DNA built into a host chromosome. They differ only in the host: prophage in bacteria, provirus in humans, episomal DNA in plants
Episomal DNA is a phage genome inside bacteria. A provirus is a herpes genome sitting beside the chromosomes. A prophage is HIV's DNA
Prophage and provirus float free in the cytoplasm as loops. Episomal DNA is the one form that is spliced into the host chromosome (herpes)

questions.explanation: Integration: prophage (bacteria) and provirus (HIV). Episomal = 'on top of' the chromosomes, not part of them (latent herpes).

questions.prompt: According to the instructor's slides, why must HIV carry reverse transcriptase?

options.text: HIV is a retrovirus with an RNA genome; reverse transcriptase turns that RNA into DNA, which is built into the host's DNA as a provirus
Reverse transcriptase is the surface protein HIV uses to bind CD4 on helper T cells
HIV has a DNA genome that must be turned into RNA before the host's ribosomes can read it
Reverse transcriptase digests the patch of host membrane that holds a budding HIV particle in place

questions.explanation: Retroviruses have RNA genomes and use reverse transcriptase to make DNA (the same enzyme used in RT-PCR, Module 14).

questions.prompt: At which stages of the viral life cycle do Tamiflu and remdesivir act?

options.text: Both act at entry — Tamiflu stops endocytosis and remdesivir stops the capsid from uncoating
Tamiflu — release (blocks neuraminidase so budding viruses can't break free); remdesivir — biosynthesis (disrupts the viral polymerase copying the genome)
Tamiflu — biosynthesis (blocks the viral polymerase); remdesivir — entry (blocks the envelope from fusing with the membrane)
Tamiflu — attachment (blocks hemagglutinin from binding receptors); remdesivir — release (blocks exocytosis from lysosomes)

questions.explanation: Tamiflu is a neuraminidase inhibitor that prevents successful budding. Remdesivir disrupts the viral polymerase.

questions.prompt: Remdesivir looks a lot like a nucleotide. Why does that matter for how it works?

options.text: It pairs with the spike protein, so the virus can no longer attach to ACE2 receptors
The viral polymerase mistakes it for a nucleotide, which disrupts genome copying and adds mutations
It is built into human DNA, where it switches off the gene for the ACE2 receptor
It forms thymine dimers in the viral genome, the same way UV light damages DNA

questions.explanation: Lecture: it 'gets in there and acts like a nucleotide and can introduce mutations into the genomes that are being replicated.'

questions.prompt: When a host cell takes in an influenza virus by endocytosis, it wraps the virus using the same kind of structure that which Module 9 organism uses to move and feed?

options.text: Euglena — a rod-stiffened flagellum
Giardia — flagella
Amoeba — pseudopods
Plasmodium — organelles at the apex

questions.explanation: Endocytosis: the host cell engulfs the virus using pseudopods — the same 'false feet' amoebas (and white blood cells) use.

questions.prompt: Which way of leaving a host cell is a normal cell process that doesn't itself damage the cell?

options.text: Exocytosis — used by SARS-CoV-2, which leaves inside lysosomes as 'waste'
Budding of influenza with the help of neuraminidase
Lysis — used by naked viruses
Budding of thousands of virions at once — used by HIV

questions.explanation: Cells release waste by exocytosis all the time. Lysis bursts the cell; mass budding strips away so much membrane that the cell likely dies.

questions.prompt: Influenza and SARS-CoV-2 are both enveloped. Where does each get its envelope?

options.text: Both build their envelopes from phospholipids encoded by genes in their own viral genomes
Influenza — from rough ER and Golgi inside the cell; SARS-CoV-2 — from the plasma membrane as it buds
Both take their envelopes from lysosome membranes as they leave the cell by exocytosis
Influenza — from the host's plasma membrane as it buds out; SARS-CoV-2 — from rough ER and Golgi membrane inside the cell, before it leaves

questions.explanation: A viral genome can't encode a phospholipid bilayer; enveloped viruses borrow host membrane — plasma membrane (budding) or ER/Golgi (SARS-CoV-2).

questions.prompt: What single idea explains BOTH why HIV infects only CD4+ helper T cells AND why phage therapy (Module 15) leaves human cells alone?

options.text: Viruses can only infect cells that have a cell wall for their tail fibers to grip
Host range is set by viral attachment proteins that must bind specific receptors on the host cell
Viruses can only enter cells that are close to their own size
Viruses only infect cells that are already damaged or dying

questions.explanation: Narrow host range: lock-and-key binding between viral proteins and specific host attachment sites.

questions.prompt: What do severe COVID and the deadliness of the 1918 flu have in common, according to the lecture?

options.text: Both killed mostly the elderly and very young, whose weaker immune systems couldn't fight the virus off
Both spread fastest among healthy adults but were stopped quickly by antiviral drugs once identified
In both, an overactive immune response caused much of the harm — in 1918, healthy people with strong immune systems died most
Both directly burst every respiratory cell they infected, so the lungs were destroyed by the virus itself

questions.explanation: Severe COVID results from an overactive immune response. In 1918, healthy people with robust immune systems had very severe hypersensitive responses.

questions.prompt: Using the lecture's numbers, about what fraction of infected people died in the 1918 flu pandemic compared with COVID worldwide (at the time of the video)?

options.text: About 1 in 5 for COVID (100 million of 536 million) versus about 1 in 85 for 1918 (6.31 million of 500 million)
About 1 in 2 for 1918 (250 million of 500 million) versus about 1 in 5 for COVID (100 million of 536 million)
About 1 in 50 for both pandemics, since the case numbers were nearly the same (about 500 million each)
About 1 in 5 for 1918 (100 million of 500 million) versus about 1 in 85 for COVID (6.31 million of 536 million)

questions.explanation: 100/500 = 20%; 6.31/536 ≈ 1.2%. Similar case numbers, very different death tolls.

questions.prompt: Which statement about acute, latent, and persistent infections is FALSE?

options.text: In a persistent infection, no virus can be detected until the productive phase begins.
Latent herpes infections can recur, with cold sores appearing again later.
In a latent infection, viral DNA stays dormant as episomal DNA before becoming productive.
A persistent HIV infection makes new viruses slowly before it may become productive.
In an acute infection, the virus immediately enters a productive phase.

questions.explanation: False — in a persistent infection new viruses are made at a very slow rate and are detectable at all times.

questions.prompt: Which statement about the influenza virus is FALSE?

options.text: Hemagglutinin helps it attach to host cells.
Its genome is a single piece of DNA.
It has a helical capsid inside an envelope.
It enters cells by endocytosis.
Neuraminidase helps budding virions break free.

questions.explanation: False — influenza has a segmented RNA genome.

questions.prompt: Follow an influenza virus from attachment to release, naming the surface proteins involved and the step where Tamiflu acts.
questions.explanation: Attachment: hemagglutinin on the envelope binds receptors on a respiratory cell (H in 'H1N1'). Entry: the cell engulfs the virus by endocytosis using pseudopods, then uncoating releases the segmented RNA genome (from the vesicle and the capsid). Biosynthesis: the host copies the viral genome and transcribes/translates viral genes; spike proteins are placed in the host's plasma membrane. Assembly: capsids form around the genome. Release: the capsid buds through the plasma membrane, taking a patch as its envelope; neuraminidase (N) digests the proteins tethering the bud so it can break free. Tamiflu inhibits neuraminidase, preventing successful budding and giving the immune system time.

questions.prompt: Explain why there are so few antiviral drugs, and how each of the course's two antivirals finds a target that our own cells don't use in the same way.
questions.explanation: Viruses are so different from living cells — they have no metabolism of their own and use the host's machinery — that there are few targets to hit without harming our cells. Tamiflu (oseltamivir) targets neuraminidase, a viral enzyme on influenza that is needed to release budding virions; blocking it stops new viruses from breaking free. Remdesivir targets the viral polymerase that copies the SARS-CoV-2 genome; it resembles a nucleotide, gets taken in during copying, and disrupts it (introducing mutations). It works best taken early.
